title: A scalable chip-integrated single-photon source array based on 50 individually addressable neutral atoms
authors: Ya-Dong Hu, Tian-Yang Zhang, Dong-Qi Ma, Yi-Chen Zhang, Liang Chen, Wen-Yi Zhu, Hong-Jie Fan, Yan-Lei Zhang, Zhu-Bo Wang, Gang Li, Xi-Feng Ren, Guang-Can Guo, Chang-Ling Zou
abstract: Scalable arrays of identical single-photon sources are a central resource for photonic quantum information processing, quantum networks and quantum metrology. Neutral atoms provide intrinsically identical emitters that can be assembled and rearranged in optical tweezers, but a many-channel fiber interface to individually trapped atoms has remained a major technical challenge. Here we demonstrate a chip-interfaced single-photon source array based on 50 individually addressable $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ atoms. A glass waveguide fan-out converts the \SI{5}{\micro m} pitch of the optical-tweezer array to the \SI{127}{\micro m} pitch of a commercial fiber array, mapping each atom to its own waveguide, fiber and single-photon detector. We resolve all 50 channels with an average nearest-neighbor cross-talk of $0.4\%$ and a uniform insertion loss of \SI{2.9}{dB}, and verify single-photon emission with $g^{(2)}(0)=0.29$, presently limited by detector dark counts and residual cooling-light scattering. Combining per-channel atom discrimination, rearrangement and reservoir replenishment, we prepare source subarrays of up to 24 atoms with a $93\%$ fill fraction. For small target numbers, atom loss is repaired from the reservoir at the detection-limited rate of \SI{118}{Hz}. We further fabricate a 784-channel waveguide chip, showing that the photonic interface can be extended well beyond the present number. This architecture establishes a fiber-native neutral-atom platform for larger arrays of identical single-photon sources.
summary: The research presents a breakthrough in creating scalable, chip-integrated single-photon source arrays using individually trapped neutral atoms. By employing a waveguide fan-out structure, the authors successfully connect the atomic array to standard fiber optics while maintaining high performance metrics like low cross-talk and confirmed single-photon emission. This establishes a robust, fiber-native platform crucial for advancing quantum information processing.
main_problem: The central challenge is developing a scalable, chip-integrated platform to generate arrays of identical single-photon sources using neutral atoms for quantum networking and computation.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an architecture that maps 50 individually addressable neutral atom sources onto a commercial fiber array with low cross-talk (0.4%) and loss (2.9 dB).
method: They utilized a glass waveguide fan-out chip interface to bridge the gap between the microscopic atomic tweezer pitch ($	ext{5 } \mu	ext{m}$) and standard optical fiber pitches ($	ext{127 } \mu	ext{m}$).
model_or_system: The system uses $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ neutral atoms trapped in an optical tweezer array. The platform is characterized by its ability to maintain high fidelity (low cross-talk, $g^{(2)}(0)=0.29$) while supporting active reservoir replenishment for sustained operation.
key_observables: Second-order correlation function ($g^{(2)}(0) = 0.29$), average nearest-neighbor cross-talk ($	ext{0.4\%}$), uniform insertion loss ($	ext{2.9 dB}$), and array reset rate ($	ext{118 Hz}$).
important_parameters: Scalability demonstrated up to $	ext{784}$ channels; source subarrays prepared with $>93\%$ fill fraction.
main_assumptions: The single-photon emission characterization is currently limited by detector dark counts and residual cooling-light scattering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the chip-interfaced waveguide fan-out, cross-talk matrices for 50 channels, confirmation of antibunching via $g^{(2)}(	au)$ measurements, and details on array preparation success rates and reset dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the necessity of scalable interfaces, detailing the chip fabrication and characterization (cross-talk, loss), confirming single-photon purity ($g^{(2)}$), and finally demonstrating active control mechanisms like reservoir replenishment to ensure sustained operation across large arrays.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck—the physical interface between quantum emitters and classical photonics infrastructure—which is essential for realizing scalable quantum networks based on neutral atoms.
